New impetus for energy
efficiency
The Roadmap was launched in June 2025 to provide renewed
political impetus and practical support to fully realise the potential
of energy efficiency as a strategic driver of affordability, industrial
competitiveness, and energy security. 
Energy efficiency is a triple win: for our climate, competitiveness, and security. Without
improvements in energy efficiency over the last 20 years, the EU’s energy consumption
today would have been about 27% higher. 
Despite the undeniable advantages of energy efficiency and the progress achieved to
date, several challenges persist, hindering progress towards the 2030 energy efficiency
targets.   
Energy efficiency roadmap – 1 year on
Commissioner for Energy and Housing,
Dan Jørgensen, reaffirmed a renewed
commitment to energy efficiency at the
IEA Global Energy Efficiency Conference
in Brussels on 13 June 2025. 
One year after its launch, the Energy
efficiency roadmap continues to support
efforts across its 10 areas of work,
focusing on simplifying implementation
of energy efficiency rules, mainstreaming
energy efficiency in EU energy policy
making and investment mobilisation. 
©European Union, 2025

1. Support and simplify implementation 
The Commission will streamline the implementation of EU energy efficiency rules in the
coming years, including the Energy Efficiency Directive, the Energy Performance of
Buildings Directive and Ecodesign and Energy Labelling. It will support EU countries with
guidance, task forces, concerted action and simplification tools to ensure effective and
aligned implementation. 
2. Mainstream energy efficiency in EU energy
policymaking
The Commission will continue to integrate energy efficiency into broader EU energy
strategies, such as the Grids Package, the Electrification Action Plan and the Heating and
Cooling Strategy, to ensure its consistent and systemic application across sectors. 
3. Strengthen sector-specific policies and product
standards   
This includes raising standards for buildings, products, data centres and heating and
cooling, by updating regulations, tackling barriers and promoting high-efficiency
solutions. 
4. Facilitate financing and investment   
The Commission continues to mobilise public and private capital with the support of the
European Investment Bank (EIB). This is achieved through coalitions, national hubs,
investment platforms, and the development of new investment tools designed to scale up
energy efficiency, such as 
the Energy Efficiency in SMEs initiative, launched in November 2025
the Clean Energy Investment Strategy, launched in March 2026 
The European Energy Efficiency Financing Coalition is also exploring new market
approaches, including 
demand activation and tailored services designed for SMEs
innovative business models for energy efficiency service providers to better reach
target groups 
5. Enhance collaboration and cooperation

Starting with the Energy Efficiency Day on 20 May 2025, the Commission pursues
structured dialogue and agreements between governments, industry and finance actors
to jointly accelerate energy efficiency implementation. 
The Efficiency Action Forum 2030, launched in December 2025, is a platform supporting
EU countries in the practical implementation of EU energy efficiency policies. It has
brought together senior officials through a series of thematic meetings, enabling the
exchange of concrete challenges, best practices and solutions, and helping to accelerate
delivery on the ground. 
At COP30 in Brazil in November 2025, the Commission and the Solar Impulse Foundation
released the joint publication Energy Efficiency: The Silent Money Maker
. It highlights
concrete and economically viable solutions to improve energy efficiency across
buildings, industry and cities, featuring real examples from EU-supported projects under
Horizon Europe, the LIFE Programme and the ELENA facility.  
6. Create a tradable energy efficiency market       
As announced in the Affordable Energy Action Plan, the Commission will explore systems
like white certificates and auctions to reward energy savings, attract investment, and turn
efficiency into a market-driven commodity. The implemented measures of the Action Plan
are listed and updated regularly.
7. Develop skills for energy efficiency
The Commission will actively support EU countries in closing the skills gap, including
through national training plans and toolkits. 
8. Boost research and innovation funding and
partnerships
The Commission will foster research and innovation in energy efficiency technologies to
drive next-generation energy efficiency solutions in buildings and industry.
9. Promote international cooperation
The Commission leverages global partnerships to spread best practices on energy-
efficient solutions in high-impact sectors, like buildings and efficient products. To deliver
on the Global Pledge, the Commission will actively promote energy efficiency at COP31,
including through collaboration with the Global South.

10. Increase energy efficiency awareness 
Energy efficiency is a policy framework that translates into tangible, meaningful
measures and actions at all levels of government. For citizens and businesses to fully
reap its benefits, they need to be well informed about the existing rights – and
obligations. This is why the Commission continues to promote the many aspects of
energy efficiency through examples, facts and figures, while striving to reach citizens,
small and medium-sized enterprises, and local communities. The LIFE publication ‘Giving
LIFE to Europe’s clean energy transition’ (February 2026) also provides good examples
through its 28 inspiring projects.
Energy efficiency awareness
The roadmap also identified 6 deliverables that were targeted for 2025–2026, focusing
on practical cooperation with EU countries and market actors.
Deliverables 2025-2026
Significant progress is being made on these actions and the key achievements include
the establishment of the Efficiency Action Forum 2030, the launch of an Energy
Efficiency for SMEs Initiative, and local collaboration via tripartite partnerships for data
centres. 
Furthermore, targeted actions are underway to boost the energy services market through
a new pilot scheme, an Electrification Action Plan and key actions on Heating and Cooling
as well as a Data Centre Energy Efficiency Package, and to mobilise dedicated financing
for SMEs and home renovations.

Portugal: linking energy efficiency with industrial competitiveness
Portugal highlighted its Sistema de Gestão dos Consumos Intensivos de Energia (SGCIE),
a mandatory energy management and audit framework for large energy-consuming
industrial operators. It shifts the paradigm of energy efficiency from a pure regulatory
burden to a powerful competitiveness tool that reduces operating costs and drives
industrial transformation. 
Key results: achieved €210 million in energy cost savings (~450 ktoe of primary energy
savings), with €17 million stemming directly from self-consumption solar PV.
Future focus: shifting attention from auxiliary systems to core industrial processes and
decarbonising thermal uses via low-temperature electrification, heat recovery, and
biomethane. 
Energy Efficiency Directive relevance: demonstrates how the directive’s provisions on
energy audits and management systems can support industrial modernisation while
enabling decarbonisation. 
Italy: a multi-level financing ecosystem
Italy presented a layered portfolio of financing instruments that support industrial
transition and energy efficiency by blending national, regional, and local initiatives. 
National level: The Development Contract (managed by MIMIT and Invitalia) backs large-
scale projects (>€20 million) with blended grants and loans, supported by the Fund for
Industrial Transition for manufacturing grants (>€3 million). 
Regional and local levels: Lombardy’s Production Chains and Industrial Ecosystems
initiative uses grants, loans, and minibonds for multi-firm collaborations, while local
chambers of commerce support smaller agro-food supply chains. 
Energy Efficiency Directive relevance: illustrates how diversified, layered financing tools
can modernise supply chains and unlock investments across companies of all sizes. 
Finland: national energy efficiency agreement scheme
In place since 1997 and running across four consecutive agreement periods, Finland’s
voluntary scheme serves as a central mechanism for fulfilling its EU energy efficiency
obligations. 
Key mechanism: utilises the Energy Efficiency Directive’s flexibility by implementing
voluntary commitments from companies, property sectors, and public entities as
alternative policy measures. 
Success factors: long-term trust, strong annual monitoring, and robust verification
systems. In 2024, the scheme provided tailored advisory services to over 220
organisations and engaged 2800 professionals.

Electrification Action Plan and Heating and
Cooling
Throughout 2025 and early 2026, the
Commission completed key procedural steps for
its upcoming Electrification Action Plan and
actions on heating and cooling. It included
extensive stakeholder consultations, dedicated
workshops on waste heat, and rigorous policy
evaluations in line with the Energy Efficiency
Directive’s Article 35(2). 
This evidence base informs both the short-term response to the energy crisis and the
long-term post-2030 structural policy framework. It aims to accelerate the deployment of
clean heat solutions for a rapid displacement of fossil fuels in heating and cooling,
focusing heavily on electrification, such as the roll-out of heat pumps, while safeguarding
consumer affordability and securing EU value chains.

To bridge the gap between public policy and
industry action, 2 key partnerships are being
deployed under the Roadmap framework,
moving at distinct stages of implementation.
Data centre integration model: On 3 June 2026, 14 European industry associations
agreed to develop an EU model for tripartite agreements between data centre operators,
energy stakeholders, and public authorities. This framework facilitates the sustainable
integration of data centres into the energy grid, notably through the reuse of waste heat
in district heating systems. 
The model will later expand to other waste-heat-producing sectors, while the European
Energy Efficiency Financing Coalition will lead reflections on project de-risking. 
Better Homes Partnership:  As a key initiative under the European Affordable Housing
Plan and the Citizen’s Energy Package, the Better Homes Partnership will accelerate
affordable, high-quality home renovations, decarbonise heating systems, and stimulate
innovative local solutions. It will act as a collaborative central point for regional
authorities, housing providers, developers, energy suppliers, and financial institutions to
pitch replicable, concrete projects that benefit from Commission endorsement to
overcome market barriers.

Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs)
face critical bottlenecks to energy renovation,
including limited internal capacity, high upfront
costs, and restricted access to capital. To solve
this, the European Commission and the EIB
Group launched the Energy Efficiency for SMEs
Initiative. The Initiative is also backed
operationally by the European Energy Efficiency
Financing Coalition, a three-party dialogue
platform between EU countries, financial
institutions, and industry.
timeline and investment target: 2025 – 2027, to mobilise €65 billion supporting
around 350 000 SMEs
delivered impact 2025: €6 billion in financing deployed, aiding up to 150 000 SMEs
banking partnerships: to set up joint financing platforms launched with intermediary
banks to scale funding
Boosting the energy services market
The European Energy Efficiency Financing
Coalition’s SME working group activates demand
and designs new business models for energy
efficiency services. The group is also finalising a
comprehensive blueprint for an SME one-stop
shop. 
In line with the Affordable Energy Action Plan and the Clean Energy Investment Strategy,
the Commission and the EIB Group are preparing a 2026 pilot scheme to fast-track "as-
a-service" business models. ‘Energy Efficiency as a Service’ is backed by the InvestEU

Data centres energy efficiency package
Aligned with the Union’s digital strategy, this
package mandates environmental transparency
from data centre operators and pushes for the
adoption of best available technologies. It is
being prepared for adoption, following the
baseline reporting scheme established in 2024,
and the comprehensive EU Tech Sovereignty
Package adopted on 3 June 2026.
The data centres package will include a 
Report to the European Parliament and Council: an exhaustive assessment of the
2024 baseline data, mapping out the pathway to a sustainable digital sector. 
Rating Scheme and label: a Delegated Regulation that automatically generates an
electronic sustainability label based on reported data, classifying data centre
performance. 
Minimum performance standards: the launch of a consultation process to phase out
inefficient technologies.
